body.text: NSW premier, opposition leader condemn planned pro-Palestinian October 7 vigils
In short:
The NSW premier and opposition leader have criticised pro-Palestinian groups that are holding vigils on the anniversary of Hamas's deadly attacks on Israel.
Organisers of the Sydney event say it also marks the day Israel launched air strikes in response.
The premier said NSW Police would "keep the public safe".
Pro-Palestinian organisations have been criticised for planning vigils for the third anniversary of the Hamas attacks on Israel, in which more than 1,200 people were killed.
Jewish organisations across the country will hold commemorations on Wednesday for those lost in the terrorist attack.
Jews Against the Occupation 48 will also hold a vigil in Sydney and Wollongong Friends of Palestine will gather "to stop and remember the martyrs and all those who suffer and continue to resist".
The organisers of the Sydney vigil are using the slogan "Don't let Israel steal the date" and said October 7 was also three years since air strikes began on Gaza in response to the attack.

They said, according to the Israel Defense Forces' timeline, its fighter jets conducted strikes in Gaza the same morning, shortly after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared that Israel was at war.
Jews Against the Occupation 48 spokesperson Michelle Berkon said the gathering would be a "solemn and peaceful vigil to commemorate the beginning of Israel's genocide against the Palestinians".

In September last year, a Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory by the UN Human Rights Council found that genocide was occurring in Gaza, an allegation vehemently rejected by Israel.
NSW Premier Chris Minns has condemned the pro-Palestine events being held on that day, labelling them "heartless" and "in poor taste".
He said he believed organisers chose the date to attract attention and feared the vigil would not prove be as peaceful as organisers may wish.
"There are some people suggesting it can be stopped, the constitution doesn't allow that," he said.
"They can certainly do that, it's not against the law but as a citizen I've got a right to make a judgement on it too."
Mr Minns added: "Police will do what they always do and that is keep the public safe."
He also asked his Labor colleagues not to attend.
"I can certainly speak for my cabinet and I can certainly speak for my senior colleagues but history has proven I can't speak for all of them," he said
"In all fairness, I don't know if anyone's [Labor MPs] going to go."
In response to the premier's remarks, member of Wollongong Friends of Palestine and vigil organiser Anke Klevjer said the event would go ahead.
"We will not allow the martyrdom of the Palestinian people to be scrubbed from this historical record of October 7," Ms Klevjer said.
'Leave that day alone'
Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-CEO Alex Ryvchin said October 7 was a "solemn day" for Jewish and Israeli communities.
"I ask those people: Leave that day alone," he said.
"Choose any other day in the calendar and carry on your obnoxious protest and divide society as you do.
"You can't be stopped, and that's fine, but this day belongs to the victims and we will remember them on that day."
Mr Ryvchin said he had been told there was concern from government such "anti-Israel" rallies like this would foster extremism and antisemitism.
He said especially in light of the Bondi Beach massacre in December last year, October 7 this year would also be remembered as an event that ushered in a new era of antisemitism.
Ms Berkon said what was "heartless" was the belief that "only some victims deserve to be mourned".
"We neither challenge nor begrudge anyone the right to mourn their dead. We simply insist on the same right for Palestinians," she said.
"As for fostering extremism, there is no evidence that the Palestine solidarity movement fosters extremism.
"In fact, our own ASIO boss has noted that the most concerning extremist views in this country are those of the far-right and other White supremacists."
'Pick any other date'
NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane told 702 ABC Sydney she found "the whole thing entirely sickening and reprehensible".
"A lot of people are very distressed by what they're seeing in Gaza and should be able to protest," she said.

"But this undermines that very intent of peace by having it on a day where 1,200 innocent people were slaughtered in the most brutal and unimaginable way, at a time when there was no retaliation by Israel."
Ms Sloane said she wanted the premier to explain how the events would be managed.
"There have been so many rallies that have been declared to be peaceful that turn out to be anything but," she said.
"We need to make sure that if that happens that we use the laws to make sure that these people are held to account."
She acknowledged that events that organisers have described as a peaceful gathering could not be banned but urged protesters to "pick any other date of the year".
"364 other dates are possible ... if you believe in peace, then please choose them," she said.
She also demanded Mr Minns order Labor MPs to stay away from the planned events.
